title: Association of a Fever Clinic Package With Waiting Time Among Walk-in Emergency Department Patients Ineligible for Fever-Clinic Streaming.
abstract:
AIM: Seasonal surges of patients with fever may delay emergency department (ED) care. This study examined whether a multicomponent fever clinic package was associated with waiting time among walk-in ED patients ineligible for fever-clinic streaming.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective before-and-after study compared year-end/new year periods in 2024-2025 and 2025-2026. The primary outcome was time from registration to first physician documentation, used as a proxy for initial physician assessment. Gamma generalized linear models were adjusted for patient characteristics, physician staffing, preceding-hour demand, study day, and arrival time. A calendar-day cluster-robust analysis and an interaction analysis between study period and arrival mode were also performed. Post-assessment throughput was exploratory.
RESULTS: Among 2056 ED visits, 793 walk-in visits ineligible for fever-clinic streaming had evaluable waiting time. Median waiting time decreased from 54 to 26 min (p < 0.001). The period with the fever clinic package was associated with shorter waiting times (adjusted mean ratio 0.57, 95% confidence interval 0.46-0.70; p < 0.001), and calendar-day cluster-robust inference was consistent with this association. The association differed by arrival mode (p for interaction < 0.001), with model-estimated waiting time decreasing among walk-in visits but not among ambulance arrivals. No consistent adjusted difference was observed in post-assessment throughput.
CONCLUSION: The period with the fever clinic package was associated with shorter waiting times among walk-in ED patients ineligible for fever-clinic streaming, without a consistent adjusted difference in post-assessment throughput. Residual between-period confounding and inseparable package components preclude causal attribution; studies with contemporaneous comparators are warranted.

title: Delayed Severe Liver Injury After Combined Acetaminophen and Iron Ingestion: Importance of Serial Reassessment in Mixed Overdose.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Assessment of combined acetaminophen and iron ingestion may be complicated when clinical manifestations, toxin concentrations, and evolving organ injury do not progress in parallel.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 12-year-old girl ingested at least 6 g of APAP (≥ 146 mg/kg) and 1 g of elemental iron (24 mg/kg). Two hours after ingestion, serum iron was 503 μg/dL while liver biochemical tests were normal. Her gastrointestinal symptoms transiently improved, but she later developed recurrent symptoms followed by severe acute liver injury and coagulopathy. At 42 h, serum iron had decreased to 219 μg/dL and APAP was < 5 μg/mL, whereas AST and ALT exceeded 5000 U/L, and PT-INR was 4.68. She received N-acetylcysteine, plasma exchange, and continuous renal replacement therapy and recovered without liver transplantation.
CONCLUSION: Serial clinical and biochemical reassessment is essential in mixed overdose when symptoms, toxin concentrations, and evolving organ injury are discordant.

title: Myeloid-Derived Suppressor Cell Trajectories in Relation to 90-Day Functional Status and PIICS After Sepsis: A Pilot Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Improved survival from sepsis has shifted attention to poor long-term outcomes among survivors. Although myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are associated with short-term mortality in sepsis, their role in long-term outcomes, including post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome, remains unclear.
METHODS: We enrolled adult patients with sepsis admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and healthy controls to examine immunological profiles in relation to long-term outcomes. MDSC frequency/phenotype and key cytokines were assessed from serial blood samples collected through Day 90 after ICU admission, using a standardized flow cytometry protocol and immunoassays, respectively. Clinical and demographic variables were retrieved from medical records. For analyses, we stratified patients by the 90-day Barthel Index after ICU admission (≥ 70 vs. < 70), reflecting dependence in activities of daily living (ADL), a core component of physical PICS.
RESULTS: This study included 14 patients with sepsis and 9 healthy volunteers. Across days 1-90, M-MDSC percentages remained higher in the poor ADL group (Barthel Index < 70) than in the good ADL group (Barthel Index ≥ 70), whereas PMN-MDSCs showed no clear between-group difference. CD86 on M-MDSCs showed time-dependent divergence between groups, whereas cytokines mainly varied over time without consistent group differences.
CONCLUSIONS: Sustained elevation of M-MDSCs, together with time-varying differences in CD86 expression on M-MDSCs, appeared to be associated with poorer physical function after sepsis, suggesting that persistent immune dysregulation may contribute to functional impairment.
CLINICAL TRIAL: The study protocol was registered in the University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN-CTR, Registration No. UMIN000041512; registration date: August 21, 2020).

title: Intravascular Ultrasound-Guided Emergency Endovascular Repair of a Tracheo-Innominate Artery Fistula for Severe Motor and Intellectual Disabilities.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tracheo-innominate artery fistula (TIF) is a lethal post-tracheostomy complication. In severe motor and intellectual disabilities, skeletal deformities and low surgical tolerance render open repair prohibitive, necessitating emergency hemostasis.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 31-year-old female with cerebral palsy developed massive tracheal hemorrhage 2 months post-tracheostomy. She presented with unstable vital signs, requiring manual syringe-push transfusion. Under cuff tamponade, emergency endovascular therapy (EVT) with Gore Viabahn and Viabahn VBX was chosen over open surgery due to thoracic deformities and limited time. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) localized the angiographically occult rupture site. Hemostasis was achieved, but suspected stent graft infection developed on Day 11 despite prophylactic antibiotic therapy. Following transition to comfort care, she died 27 days post-procedure due to anemia, hypotension, and impaired ventilation.
CONCLUSION: Emergency IVUS-guided EVT under cuff tamponade is a valuable life-saving strategy and potential definitive treatment option for TIF in patients with prohibitive surgical risk, though late-onset infection remains a critical challenge.

title: Sympathetic Hyperactivity in the Recovery Phase of Severe Tetrodotoxin Poisoning: A Case Report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tetrodotoxin poisoning can cause hypotension through peripheral sympathetic blockade. A case of paroxysmal tachycardia, hypertension, and fever suggestive of sympathetic hyperactivity during recovery from severe poisoning is reported.
CASE PRESENTATION: A woman in her 70s with hypertension developed respiratory arrest after eating pufferfish liver and required mechanical ventilation. Neurological recovery began on Day 4, accompanied by recurrent tachycardia, hypertension, and fever. Heart rate reached 154 bpm and temperature reached 40.2°C on Day 8. After propranolol initiation on Day 8, tachycardia and fever episodes lessened, although intermittent blood pressure elevations persisted. Propranolol was gradually tapered and discontinued on Day 23. She was discharged home on Day 50.
CONCLUSION: Sympathetic hyperactivity may complicate neurological recovery from severe tetrodotoxin poisoning. Propranolol initiation was temporally associated with reduced tachycardia and fever, but the underlying mechanism and treatment effect are unclear.

Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Challenging airways are common in the out-of-hospital setting, where delays or failure to secure the airway can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, this pilot study aimed to determine whether training paramedics in the role of airway assistant improves intubation time during a simulated regurgitating airway using suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination (SALAD).
METHODS: Twelve qualified paramedics were randomly allocated to one of two groups (n = 6) and paired with intensive care paramedics (ICPs). Airway assistants in Group 1 completed a one-hour airway assistant training program, whereas airway assistants in Group 2 received no training. Participants completed a standardized, timed simulation using a continuously regurgitating mannequin designed to replicate the challenges of out-of-hospital intubation. The primary outcome was time to successful intubation, defined as passage of the endotracheal tube through the vocal cords with cuff inflation.
RESULTS: Airway assistant training significantly reduced intubation time. The untrained group recorded a median intubation time of 102.5 seconds (IQR 36), compared with 53 seconds (IQR 19) in the trained group. Group comparisons demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in intubation time (p = 0.009) and corresponded to a very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86; Hedges' g = 1.72). No association was observed between intubation time and the age or experience of either the airway assistant or the ICP. No esophageal intubations occurred in either group.
CONCLUSIONS: In this pilot study, training paramedics to perform the airway assistant role significantly reduced intubation time in a simulated regurgitating airway. These preliminary findings suggest that incorporating structured airway assistant training into prehospital education programs may improve airway management performance in challenging environments. Given the small sample size and simulated setting, larger studies are required to confirm these findings and determine whether the observed benefits translate to clinical practice.

title: Positive pressure ventilation in newborns at birth: a systematic review of recipient characteristics and temporal trends.
abstract:
AIM: To synthesise evidence on temporal trends, recipient characteristics and variation in the use of positive pressure ventilation (PPV) at birth.
METHODS: This systematic review was registered (CRD42024487025) and followed a condition-context-population framework. Five electronic databases and grey literature were searched to 25 June 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using the JBI checklist, and reporting followed PRISMA 2020.
RESULTS: Forty-two studies from 34 countries (27 from high-income countries), reporting 269 to 10,696,831 livebirths per study (1984-2024), were included. Heterogeneity in whether continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) was distinguished from PPV, interface definitions and eligibility criteria precluded meta-analysis. Fifteen studies included only preterm infants and 19 excluded congenital anomalies. Nine population-based and large multicentre studies that excluded CPAP and included all age groups reported PPV incidence ranging from 3.0% to 8.0%. Rates were much higher among very and extremely preterm infants. Temporal trends suggested increasing PPV incidence overall and via facemask, whereas tracheal-tube PPV was stable or declining. Lower PPV incidence was reported in low-resource and lower-level birthing centres. Few studies reported indications for or timing of PPV initiation, and reported data items were inconsistent.
CONCLUSIONS: PPV remains common in neonatal resuscitation, with higher use at lower gestational ages and higher-level birthing services. Limited and heterogeneous reporting of indications and PPV timelines constrains interpretation and comparison. Standardised, neonatal Utstein-aligned reporting, including PPV indications and time intervals and separate reporting of airway interfaces and CPAP, is needed. Further population-based studies, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, are warranted.

title: Coronary Perfusion Pressure During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation is Associated with Outcomes from Pediatric In-hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multiple animal studies and one adult study establish that coronary perfusion pressure (CoPP) during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is associated with survival outcomes, such as return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Yet, CoPP during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) has not been investigated. We hypothesized that an average CoPP ≥20mmHg during the first 10 minutes of CPR for pIHCA would be associated with higher rates of ROSC.
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of the ICU-RESUScitation trial, a cluster randomized, step-wedged trial of a physiology-focused quality improvement bundle in pIHCA. Index CPR events among patients ≥37 weeks corrected gestational age and <18 years with invasive arterial blood pressure (BP) and central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring were eligible for inclusion. The primary exposure was event-level average CoPP (≥20mmHg vs <20mmHg) during the first 10 minutes of CPR; secondary exposure was CoPP <10 mmHg. The primary outcome was sustained ROSC ≥20 minutes. Multivariable modified Poisson regression with adjustment for confounders evaluated the relationship between CoPP and outcomes.
RESULTS: Among 111 included patients, median age was 0.2 years [0.0, 0.6]. Seventy-one (64%) achieved ROSC. Thirty (27%) had CoPP ≥20mmHg. Patients with CoPP ≥20mmHg were more frequently ≥1 year of age and less frequently had congenital heart disease. In adjusted models, average CoPP ≥20mmHg was associated with higher rates of ROSC (aRR 1.48 [95%CI 1.12, 1.95]; p=0.005). CoPP <10 mmHg was associated with lower rates of ROSC.
CONCLUSIONS: In this first investigation of CoPP during CPR for pIHCA, CoPP ≥20mmHg was associated with ROSC.

title: Cycle-to-Cycle Prediction of Return of Spontaneous Circulation Using End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Dynamics in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prognostication in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) commonly relies on static pre-resuscitation variables, although resuscitation is a rapidly evolving physiologic process. End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) is continuously available during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but its sequential information has not been fully used for real-time prediction. We aim to develop and internally validate a cycle-to-cycle time-updated prediction model using sequential EtCO2 values to estimate the probability of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) in the subsequent 2-minute resuscitation cycle.
METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of adult OHCA patients from the NTUH-HYCARD database between 2016 and 2023. Event-level EtCO2 sequences were extracted from resuscitation records and standardized into 2-minute intervals for up to 30 minutes, consistent with Advanced Cardiac Life Support reassessment cycles. At each prediction time point, the model used EtCO2 values available from event onset to the current time point, without using future values. A two-layer long short-term memory model estimated the probability of ROSC in the subsequent cycle. Performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation at two levels: the event level (one prediction per event) and the cycle level (one prediction per 2-minute cycle).
RESULTS: The final analysis included 1,651 event-level EtCO2 sequences from 1,480 patients; 583 events ended with ROSC. At the event level, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.876 (95% CI, 0.863-0.890) and a Brier score of 0.140 (95% CI, 0.131-0.149). When applied to every 2-minute cycle (17,029 prediction points; ROSC prevalence, 3.4%), the AUROC was 0.685 (95% CI, 0.664-0.706), and the model systematically overestimated ROSC probability (Brier score, 0.285; 95% CI, 0.268-0.303).
CONCLUSION: Sequential EtCO2 dynamics showed good event-level discrimination for predicting ROSC in the subsequent cycle. When applied at each cycle, the model retained modest discrimination but overestimated ROSC probability, indicating that recalibration is required before cycle-to-cycle use.

title: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (TCA) has extremely poor outcomes, and the benefit of prehospital advanced airway management (AAM) remains uncertain, partly because previous observational studies may have been affected by resuscitation time bias. We examined the association between prehospital AAM and clinical outcomes in adults with TCA using a time-dependent analytic approach.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective observational cohort study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency medical services transport records from 2021 to 2023. Adults (≥18 years) with TCA were included. The exposure was successful prehospital AAM, including supraglottic airway placement or endotracheal intubation. The primary outcome was 30-day survival, and the secondary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2) at 30 days. We applied time-dependent propensity score sequential matching and estimated corrected risk differences (RDs) using generalized estimating equations with inverse-frequency weighting.
RESULTS: Among 7,217 patients, 2,653 (36.8%) received prehospital AAM, of whom 2,637 were successfully matched within the analytic cohort. Thirty-day survival was 1.8% in the AAM group and 1.4% among matched controls (corrected RD, 0.6%; 95% confidence interval (CI), -0.1 to 1.2). Favorable neurological outcome occurred in 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively (corrected RD, -0.2%; 95% CI, -0.6 to 0.1). No significant timing-dependent association or prespecified subgroup heterogeneity was observed.
CONCLUSIONS: In this nationwide cohort study using time-dependent propensity score sequential matching, prehospital AAM was not significantly associated with improved outcomes in adults with TCA.

title: Early Watery Diarrhea and Intestinal Injury Assessed by I-FABP Are Associated With Poor Outcomes in Heat Stroke: A Single-Center Observational Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: We aimed to clarify the relationship between intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP) levels, intestinal injury, and clinical outcomes in patients with heat stroke.
METHODS: We conducted an observational study of patients with heat stroke admitted between 2021 and 2024. Patient characteristics and the occurrence of watery diarrhea within 24 h of admission were compared according to serum I-FABP levels measured on admission. Poor outcomes were defined as death or ongoing hospitalization at 90 days after admission. ROC curve analysis was used to assess associations among I-FABP levels, watery diarrhea, and poor outcomes.
RESULTS: A total of 58 patients were included, of whom 9 (15.5%) experienced poor outcomes. Watery diarrhea was observed in 10 patients (17.2%). I-FABP levels were higher in patients with severe heat stroke than in those with non-severe heat stroke (108.1 ng/mL [4.2-223.2] vs. 2.8 ng/mL [1.6-5.0]). Patients who developed watery diarrhea showed markedly elevated I-FABP levels (205.9 ng/mL [16.7-256.1]). ROC analysis demonstrated that I-FABP levels on admission predicted watery diarrhea with an area under the curve of 0.881.
CONCLUSIONS: Watery diarrhea within 24 h of admission was strongly associated with poor outcomes in patients with heat stroke. Serum I-FABP levels measured on admission may serve as an adjunctive biomarker reflecting intestinal injury and disease severity.

Pooled prevalence of infectious diseases among first responders in the prehospital setting: A systematic review with meta-analysis by occupation.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers.
METHODS: Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I², τ², and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool.
RESULTS: Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%- 5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonisation. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%- 25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%- 12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039.
CONCLUSIONS: Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

title: Prehospital Whole Blood Resuscitation in Pediatric Patients: A San Antonio Cohort Descriptive.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study is to describe the demographic, clinical, and prehospital care characteristics of pediatric patients receiving whole blood (WB) resuscitation by San Antonio Fire Department (SAFD).
METHODS: We conducted an observational retrospective cohort study to evaluate pediatric patients who received prehospital low-titer group O positive WB transfusion through the SAFD prehospital blood program between October 2018 and June 2025. The objective was to characterize patient demographics, injury patterns, resuscitative interventions, shock physiology, and outcomes among pediatric recipients in a mature civilian emergency medical services WB program.
RESULTS: Of 1703 WB transfusions, 73 (4.3%) were pediatric. Most patients were male (76%), age range 1-17 years old with a mode of 17 years, adolescents represented 78%. Trauma accounted for 96% of cases, firearm injury (74%); all penetrating (84%), blunt (12%), with the remainder classified as medical/unknown. Vascular access was intravenous (73%), intraosseous (26%). Tranexamic acid was co-administered in 39%; 12% received ceftriaxone. When analyzed using age-adjusted Shock Index Pediatric Age-Adjusted (SIPA) thresholds (>1.2 for 1-6 years, >1.0 for 7-12 years, and >0.9 for 13-17 years), based on the initial available prehospital heart rate and systolic blood pressure, 45% of patients had an elevated SIPA, 22% had a normal SIPA, 20% were pulseless and therefore could not undergo SIPA calculation, and 14% lacked sufficient vital-sign data for classification. Survival was 50%; died 39%, and unknown outcomes 11%. Mean delta shock index values were most negative in toddlers (1-4 years) -0.97 ± 1.29, followed by children (5-11 years) -0.76 ± 1.07 and adolescents (12-17 years) -0.16 ± 0.46, indicating a greater physiologic response to resuscitation among younger pediatric patients.
CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric WB recipients were predominantly adolescent males who sustained penetrating trauma and presented with moderate-to-severe shock. Younger age groups had larger descriptive decreases in shock index during the prehospital encounter; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small subgroup sizes and observational design.

title: Airway management during missions of a neurologist-staffed mobile stroke unit: a retrospective registry study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Following their endorsement by international guidelines, mobile stroke units (MSUs) are increasingly being integrated into emergency medical services worldwide. In real-world use, physician-staffed MSUs can be dispatched beyond their intended indication, exposing on-board neurologists to non-stroke emergencies. This raises important clinical and regulatory questions about the competencies MSU physicians need. Advanced airway management is one of the most critical prehospital interventions. Yet, its frequency, indications, procedural characteristics and success rates have not been investigated in neurologist-staffed MSU services.
METHODS: We retrospectively analysed a prospective registry of mission documentation from a neurologist-staffed MSU service in Berlin, Germany from 31 August 2024 to 15 March 2026. Dispatches of the MSU were classified as stroke or non-stroke dispatches using the recorded activation code. The primary outcome was the dispatch-based frequency of endotracheal intubation (ETI), defined as a documented intubation attempt. All ETIs were performed by the on-board neurologist. Secondary outcomes included supraglottic airway (SGA) use, first-pass success rate, procedural characteristics and self-reported post-mission National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) workload. Proportions are reported with 95% Wilson confidence intervals (CI).
RESULTS: We analysed 3,887 dispatches. ETI occurred in a total of 49 dispatches (1.26%; 95% CI 0.95-1.66) with 2 in 1,755 stroke- (0.11%; 95% CI 0.03-0.41) and 47 in 2,132 non-stroke dispatches (2.20%; 95% CI 1.66-2.92). SGA use occurred in 22 dispatches (0.57%; 95% CI 0.37-0.86). All 49 intubation attempts were successful (100.0%; 95% CI 92.7-100.0). First-pass success was achieved in 43/49 (87.8%; 95% CI 75.8-94.3) with no ETI requiring more than two attempts. Videolaryngoscopy was used in all ETIs and capnographic confirmation of tube position in 48/49 (98%). Non-traumatic cardiac arrest was the most frequent indication (30/49). In the exploratory workload analysis, the median NASA-TLX score was 59.8 [IQR 50.0-68.7] in 49 dispatches with ETI and 27.0 [15.5-41.7] in 2,700 dispatches without ETI.
CONCLUSIONS: ETI was infrequent overall and particularly rare during stroke dispatches, yet first-pass success was high. Prospective studies are needed to define airway management requirements and training standards for MSU physicians.

title: From Rescue to Donation: Embedding Ethics into the ECPR Outcomes Framework.
Emergency Response and Patient Transport in Remote Indigenous Communities: A Scoping Review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Prehospital and inter-facility transport, such as air medical retrieval and pre-birth evacuation, often move Indigenous patients in rural and remote settings out of their communities, where care is already shaped by fragmented funding and structural inequities; no review has mapped these pathways globally. This scoping review mapped evidence on prehospital emergency response and patient transport for this population.
METHODS: A librarian-assisted PubMed, Embase, and Scopus search was conducted for English-language publications on March 9, 2026. Eligible studies included an explicit rural Indigenous population with a defined prehospital pathway. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts, and a third reviewer resolved disagreements. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively.
RESULTS: Across eight countries, 76 studies met the inclusion criteria, primarily from Australia (n = 29) and Canada (n = 23). Air transport and medical evacuation was the most frequently described pathway (71%), followed by ground transport (51%). Explicit description of paramedic or emergency medical services (24%) and dispatch/9-1-1 (12%) were depicted less frequently. Additionally, pathways were commonly described but rarely evaluated: only 12/76 (16%) publications used an evaluative design, and no pathway was evaluated in more than 7 of 76 publications (9%). The most reported barriers were infrastructure and communications (92%), cost and jurisdiction (87%), and distance to definitive care (83%). All percentages describe how often a topic was reported across the 76 included publications, and not its prevalence in practice. An explicit cultural-safety framework was applied in 9% of the publications, and community-led governance of the research in 7%.
CONCLUSIONS: The published evidence disproportionately described transporting patients out of their communities. Community first response and tele-support were described more often than their standing in the literature suggests; however, they were rarely evaluated, and Indigenous-led governance of the research itself was reported in 7% of publications. Low reporting frequency does not establish that these models are uncommon in application and practice. Future priorities include community-partnered evaluation of community-based capacity and telehealth-supported care, alongside the development of patient and family cultural safety.

Initial shockable rhythm detection among patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest by arrest location: A population-based cohort study in Japan.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: We described the patient characteristics, bystander interventions, and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) according to arrest location, focusing on initial rhythm and automated external defibrillator (AED) use.
METHODS: We analyzed medical-origin OHCAs from a population-based registry (2016-2024) by arrest location: home, nursing home, or other locations. Patient characteristics, bystander interventions, and outcomes were summarized descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression examined the association between arrest location and initial shockable rhythm.
RESULTS: Among 2478 OHCA cases, initial shockable rhythm was identified in 36.3% (221/609) in nursing homes, 7.1% (113/1582) at home, and 33.4% (96/287) in other locations. After adjustment, the odds of an initial shockable rhythm were higher in nursing homes than at home (adjusted OR, 12.35; 95% CI, 8.93-17.24) and than in other locations (adjusted OR, 2.35; 95% CI, 1.60-3.45). In nursing homes, 96.8% (214/221) of patients with an initial shockable rhythm received an AED shock. One-month survival with favorable neurological outcomes was the lowest in nursing homes (0.8% [5/609]).
CONCLUSIONS: Initial shockable rhythm was identified in more than one-third of arrests occurring in nursing homes, and 97% of these patients received an AED shock. This finding may partly reflect earlier AED access, potentially increasing the likelihood of detecting a shockable rhythm soon after collapse. These findings underscore the importance of early rhythm detection through prompt AED use and suggest that extending AED access to home settings warrants further investigation.

title: Quantifying discrepancies between EMS time intervals in the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and emergency medical dispatch data: a 10-year analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess discrepancies between time intervals reported to the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (SRCR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and those recorded by the dispatch centre between 2015 and 2024.
METHODS: In this retrospective observational study, OHCAs reported to the registry were linked to dispatch centre data to correct and validate EMS case numbers. Time interval discrepancies were quantified by comparing the EMS dispatch-to-arrival interval (unit response time) with the call start-to-arrival interval (total response time). Differences between the two sources were estimated using Bayesian quantile regression by modelling the median response-time distribution.
RESULTS: Among 56,969 registry records, 1004 (1.8%) lacked an EMS case number. On a pooled national level, unit response time showed negligible discrepancies between the two sources, with a median difference of 0.3 s (95% CrI -4.1 to 3.9). In contrast, the total response time was systematically shorter in the registry, with a median difference of -80.9 s (95% CrI -84.7 to -77.1). Both time intervals showed large regional variation, with the smallest difference in the Stockholm region.
CONCLUSION: On a pooled national level, unit response time showed high concordance, whereas total response time was systematically shorter in the registry. Registry time variables, particularly total response time, should be interpreted with caution when evaluating small performance differences.

title: Intra-arrest blood pressure monitoring during paediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
AIM: To evaluate the use of intra-arrest blood pressure monitoring and association between blood pressure thresholds and outcomes in infants and children.
METHODS: A systematic review was performed, registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024590080). We executed the search strategy on MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials all years until April 1, 2026. We used GRADE and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale to assess the evidence found. Critically important outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital discharge, and survival with favourable neurological outcome, as defined in the Paediatric Core Outcome Set for Cardiac Arrest.
RESULTS: Six studies were included in the final analysis. Two studies (577 events) were pooled. A diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of ≥25 mmHg for infants <1 year and ≥30 mmHg for children 1-≤18 years, averaged over the first ten minutes of CPR, was associated with improved rates of ROSC, survival to hospital discharge, and survival with favourable neurological outcome, with very low certainty of evidence. The analysis did not find a statistically significant association for intra-arrest systolic blood pressure (SBP) thresholds and the described outcomes.
CONCLUSION: In infants and children with invasive arterial monitoring in place during IHCA, a DBP of ≥25 mmHg (infants) or ≥30 mmHg (children) during the first 10 min of CPR was associated with improved survival and neurological outcome. The evidence is observational and of very low certainty, and does not establish that titrating resuscitation to these thresholds improves outcomes.The protocol for this systematic review was registered as PROSPERO ID CRD42024590080.

title: The first survivor's voice: breaking the silence of the public on cardiopulmonary resuscitation in Somaliland, East Africa.
Experiences and coping strategies of bystanders involved in out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a qualitative study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Participating in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can have a substantial emotional and psychological impact on bystanders. Understanding their experiences and coping strategies may inform supportive interventions that could mitigate the impact on future bystanders.
METHODS: The study used a qualitative research design grounded in an experiential orientation. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with people who had been involved in CPR during an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in Scotland outside of a professional role. Participants were recruited via social media advertisements. We transcribed and analysed interviews using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Eleven interviews were conducted between November 2024 and April 2025. Most bystanders knew the person (n = 9, 81%) as a family member, team member or neighbour. Most were female (n = 9, 82%) and were non-healthcare professionals (n = 7, 64%). Seven of those who experienced OHCA survived, three died, and one outcome was unknown. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four interconnected themes: Emotional impact; Managing multiple roles and responsibilities; Compelled to help but unprepared; and Talking to the right person.
CONCLUSION: Findings from the interviews with bystanders suggest that OHCA can have a substantial emotional impact, particularly when the person dies or is known to the bystander. Several ways to reduce this impact were identified, including greater emotional preparation in CPR training, involvement in activities that prepare themselves or others for OHCA/CPR, and opportunities to speak with an independent person knowledgeable about OHCA/CPR. Future research should investigate the effectiveness of incorporating these strategies into support interventions for OHCA bystanders.

title: Translation and validation of the TEAM-NL instrument for assessing interprofessional team performance in simulation-based resuscitation training.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Effective interprofessional teamwork is essential for successful resuscitation care. The Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) is widely used to assess emergency team performance; however, a validated Dutch version is lacking. This study aimed to translate and validate a Dutch version of the TEAM (TEAM-NL) for simulation-based resuscitation training.
METHODS: A structured cross-cultural adaptation was performed, including forward-backward translation, developer review and expert review. Instructors used the TEAM-NL during Advanced Life Support courses at two Dutch training centres, rating each participant group in two simulation scenarios. Internal consistency, inter-rater reliability, convergent validity, change in scores between scenarios, acceptability and score distribution were assessed.
RESULTS: A total of 52 participant groups were observed, yielding 104 observed team performances and 299 instructor ratings. The mean total score (range 0-44) was 32.1 (SD 6.9). Internal consistency was high (Cronbach's α = 0.93). Inter-rater reliability was moderate for two raters (ICC(1,2) = 0.68, 95% CI 0.53-0.79) and good for three raters (ICC(1,3) = 0.78, 95% CI 0.69-0.85). The total score correlated strongly with the global performance rating (r = 0.86, p < 0.001). Scores were higher in the second scenario (mean difference 4.3, 95% CI 2.2-6.4; dz  = 0.57). Missing data were minimal (0-2.7% per item). No floor effects were observed; ceiling effects were present for all items (19.4-36.1%).
CONCLUSION: The TEAM-NL showed high internal consistency, convergent validity and acceptability for instructor-based assessment of team performance during simulation-based resuscitation training. Inter-rater reliability was moderate for two raters and good when the ratings of three instructors were averaged.

title: Infant carry sling-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and other circumstances surrounding such events in children under two years: A five-year regional registry analysis.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Infant carry slings are widely used for infant transport and bonding. However, concerns regarding safety have been raised, including risks of positional asphyxia from improper use, particularly in younger infants. This service evaluation explored the frequency of infant carry sling-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in children under two years old over a five-year period within a regional English ambulance service, placing these findings within the wider epidemiological context.
METHODS: This retrospective observational service evaluation used data from an existing OHCA registry and included all patients aged under 2 years who received a resuscitation attempt following cardiac arrest between 1 April 2020 and 31 March 2025. Free-text narratives were reviewed to identify circumstances associated with OHCA, with particular attention paid to carry sling-associated OHCAs.
RESULTS: A total of 162 OHCA incidents in children aged under two years were identified, representing 1.0% of all resuscitation attempts during the five-year period. This included 114 infants aged under one year (excluding neonatal life support patients, n = 28). Only two carry sling-associated incidents were identified, both occurring in patients under one year, representing 1.8% of infant OHCAs. The most frequently documented circumstances surrounding OHCA were co-sleeping (33.3%) and patients found unresponsive (e.g. in a cot, bed, sofa or pushchair) (26.3%).
CONCLUSIONS: Only two carry sling-associated OHCA incidents were identified over five years, suggesting such events were uncommon within this regional registry. In contrast, other sleep-related circumstances, particularly co-sleeping, accounted for a substantially larger proportion of infant OHCA cases.

title: The use of real-time CPR quality feedback prompts during in-hospital cardiac arrest in medical intensive care: uptake and barriers, a single-center cross-sectional study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) improves survival after in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). Real-time audio and visual CPR quality feedback may improve CPR quality, but real-world use and uptake are incompletely understood. We evaluated awareness, use, and barriers to defibrillator-integrated CPR feedback among Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU) clinicians.
METHODS: We used a cross-sectional study design. An anonymous REDCap survey was distributed to nurses, advanced practice providers (APPs), and physicians across three adult MICUs at a single urban academic medical center in February 2024. Respondents reported usual IHCA roles (chest compressor, code leader, CPR coach), familiarity with the Zoll R Series defibrillator's visual and audio feedback functions, use of feedback during real IHCA events, and role-specific perceived barriers.
RESULTS: Seventy-nine clinicians responded of the 413 invited, 54% by nurses and 43% by physicians. 94% reported involvement in an IHCA during the past year and 92% had received defibrillator training. Awareness of visual and audio feedback functions was 57% and 72%, respectively. Among those aware, 10% often or always looked at the screen for visual feedback while performing chest compressions, 37% while leading a code, and 57% as CPR coach. Audio feedback use was higher 46%, 58%, 50%. Reported barriers during IHCA events included screen placement, reliance on others to monitor visual feedback, and difficulty hearing auditory feedback.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center survey, uptake of integrated CPR feedback during IHCA was incomplete despite near-universal training, and barriers varied by role during IHCA.

Non-urgent emergency department utilization in adults: a systematic review of associated factors across diverse health systems.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Non-urgent emergency department (ED) visits represent a growing global challenge with significant economic and operational consequences. Despite previous reviews, important gaps remain. No review has included all commonly used terms for non-urgent ED visits, recent evidence has not been synthesised, and factors related to patients, health systems, and care contexts have rarely been examined together. This systematic review aimed to identify and categorize factors associated with non-urgent ED visits in adults.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published between January 2015 and May 2026. We included cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies that compared urgent and non-urgent ED visits and reported at least one associated factor. Quality assessment was performed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists. Because of substantial heterogeneity in definitions, the findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Thirty-two studies from 21 countries were included. The proportion of non-urgent visits ranged from 1% to 82.4%, depending on the definition and measurement approach used. Five approaches were used to define non-urgent visits. The most common were triage-based (41%) and clinical judgment-based (28%). Associated factors were classified into three main categories: (1) demographic and socioeconomic (younger age, female sex, low income, lower education, non-native nationality); (2) access and health system (self-referral, arrival on foot, weekend visits, shorter distance to ED, lack of a family physician, public insurance); and (3) clinical and perceptual (non-specific diagnosis, musculoskeletal problems, mental health conditions, prior ED visit history, and patient perception of illness severity). The strongest associations were reported for frequent previous ED visits (aOR up to 82.13) and patients who perceived their illness as non-serious (aOR up to 21.03).
CONCLUSION: Non-urgent ED visits are influenced by multiple individual, health system, and perceptual factors. The substantial heterogeneity in definitional approaches underscores the need for conceptual standardization. No single intervention is likely to reduce non-urgent ED visits. Effective strategies should strengthen primary care, improve insurance policies, increase public health education, and empower patients.

title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024).
PATIENTS: Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold.
CONCLUSIONS: ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

title: Neurological Outcomes of Rhythm Transitions in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Initial Nonshockable Rhythms: A Nationwide Population-Based Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the prognostic implications of rhythm transitions between asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with initial nonshockable rhythms.
DESIGN: Nationwide population-based observational study.
SETTING: Nationwide OHCA Registry of South Korea, managed by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
PATIENTS: Consecutive adult (≥ 18 yr old) OHCA patients with nonshockable rhythms from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2021.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Patients were categorized into four groups based on rhythm changes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): asystole-to-asystole (A-A), asystole-to-PEA (A-P), PEA-to-asystole (P-A), and PEA-to-PEA (P-P). The primary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1-2. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to adjust for measured confounding. In the primary IPTW model, weighted risks of good neurologic outcome were 0.101% in A-A, 0.231% in A-P, 0.384% in P-A, and 0.874% in P-P. Compared with A-A, the odds of good neurologic outcome were higher in A-P (odds ratio [OR], 2.28; 95% CI, 1.78-2.93; risk difference [RD], 0.130 percentage points), P-A (OR, 3.80; 95% CI, 3.01-4.80; RD, 0.283 percentage points), and P-P (OR, 8.70; 95% CI, 6.98-10.83; RD, 0.773 percentage points). Compared with A-P, P-A had higher odds of good neurologic outcome (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.39-1.99; RD, 0.153 percentage points).
CONCLUSIONS: Asystole conversion to PEA during CPR was associated with a better neurologic outcome than persistent asystole. Although transitioning from PEA to asystole was associated with lower odds of a good outcome compared with persistent PEA, it was associated with a better outcome than A-P transitions. Recognizing these patterns may provide prognostic context beyond a single rhythm assessment.

title: The Impact of Hospital Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Volume and Its Distribution Across ICUs on Adult Patients' Outcomes: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Research from a prior era of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) found that higher hospital ECMO volume was associated with higher survival rates, but it did not examine whether distributing ECMO volume across multiple ICUs affected this relationship.
DESIGN: Retrospective analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry.
SETTING: ECMO centers contributing to the registry.
PATIENTS: Adult patients required ECMO support from 2012 to 2023.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We analyzed adult patients from the ELSO registry (2012-2023), adjusting for hospital factors and case mix using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression. The main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Hospital experience was measured by the annual number of adult ECMO cases and total ECMO hours. Volume-outcome associations were modeled for all centers and by total adult ICUs per center. We included 115,849 adults on ECMO across 495 hospitals. Model estimates showed small decreases in mortality odds with higher annual case counts (odds ratio [OR], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97-0.99 per 10-case increase) and ECMO hours (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr increase). Hospitals with one ICU had a median of 10 cases (interquartile interval [IQI], 3-25 cases), while those with four or more ICUs had a median of 50 (IQI, 28-91). Adjusted mortality was higher in centers delivering ECMO across four+ ICUs compared with one ICU (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06-1.31), the annual case model (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.26), and the annual ECMO hours model. Higher volume was associated with a reduction in the odds of mortality for hospitals with four+ ICUs compared with those with one ICU (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96-1.00 per 10 cases and OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr).
CONCLUSIONS: Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with reduced mortality. Hospitals with more adult ICUs that perform ECMO may experience higher mortality, which may be explained by increased patient complexity and is offset by the higher center volume. More research is needed to better understand the optimum design of ECMO centers.

title: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but evidence from randomized trials about whether community-based implementation strategies improve outcomes is lacking.
METHODS: We conducted a registry-based, cluster-randomized trial involving adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by emergency medical services (EMS) in North Carolina counties. The counties were grouped into clusters, which were then randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to implement a multifaceted intervention or administer usual care. The intervention included four components: training of 911 telecommunicators to improve rapid recognition of cardiac arrest, training of 911 telecommunicators to improve delivery of CPR instructions from telecommunicators to bystanders, community CPR training, and enhanced use of automated external defibrillators by first responders or bystanders before EMS arrival. Data were collected through the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome (Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2; range, 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating worse neurologic outcome).
RESULTS: From July 1, 2022, to June 30, 2026, a total of 28 clusters comprising 11,615 patients were assigned to the intervention group, and 27 clusters comprising 10,844 patients were assigned to the usual-care group. The median age of the patients was 64.0 years, and 36.7% were women. The percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome was 9.0% (1048 of 11,608 patients) in the intervention group and 9.4% (1017 of 10,839 patients) in the usual-care group (adjusted odds ratio, 0.97; 95% confidence interval, 0.75 to 1.26; P = 0.80).
CONCLUSIONS: Among adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, implementation of a multifaceted strategy involving the community and EMS did not result in a greater percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome than usual care. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health; RACE-CARS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04660526.).

title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited.
METHODS: In a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge.
RESULTS: A total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group.
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. (Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health; OnScene ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04620070.).

title: An Emergency Department and Emergency Medical Services Superutilizer - A Case Report of a Multidisciplinary Approach to Resolution.
abstract: Frequent emergency department (ED) visitors, referred to as high-need, high-cost, or "superutilizers," are a challenging population for the health care system. Superutilizers account for a disproportionate share of overall health care spending (5% of the population accounts for 50% of health care spending) and have therefore been a focus of research and intervention over the past decade. Although ED superutilizers have been described previously, we report a case that demonstrates the additional strain on the emergency medical services (EMS). A 65-year-old woman was the highest 9-1-1 caller for a major metropolitan area, averaging 1.6 transports per day. Identifying the root causes of a patient's frequent utilization can be difficult and sometimes requires stepping back, gaining a fresh perspective, or returning to basic questions, including "why is this patient failing home therapy?" In this case, undetected cognitive impairment was a significant contributor to her frequent utilization. A hospital/EMS paramedicine partnership facilitated detection and care for this root cause and stopped the frequent ED and 9-1-1 use. This case highlights the impact of superutilizers on EMS, the promising role of intervention teams, and the complexity of cognition/capacity determination in the ED.

title: The global research landscape of emergency medical services in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major cause of death, and emergency medical services (EMS) are central to recognition, resuscitation, transport, and linkage to post-arrest care. Although previous bibliometric studies have mapped the broader cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation literature, the intersection of EMS and OHCA warrants focused characterization.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective bibliometric analysis of records indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 1972 through June 2026. The search combined OHCA terms with terms for EMS, paramedics, and emergency medical technicians. Annual output, research categories, journals, authors, and countries were described. VOSviewer version 1.6.20 was used for author co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and cited-reference co-citation analyses.
RESULTS: The search identified 3,005 records. Annual output increased markedly after 2010, peaked at 244 publications in 2021, and remained above 200 publications per year from 2022 to 2025; 130 records were indexed for the partial 2026 year. Emergency Medicine (1,745; 58.1%) and Critical Care Medicine (1,014; 33.7%) were the most frequently assigned Web of Science categories. Resuscitation published 694 records (23.1%). The United States had the greatest country-level output (1,022; 34.0%), followed by Japan (375; 12.5%) and Canada (281; 9.4%). The most prolific author was Shin SD (98 publications). Co-authorship mapping showed registry-centered regional communities, while keyword analysis yielded ten interpreted domains spanning epidemiology, resuscitation interventions, dispatch, registries, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, equity, and technology-related topics. Co-citation analysis identified four major intellectual communities.
CONCLUSION: EMS-focused OHCA publications indexed in Web of Science show sustained output and international collaboration associated with established registries. Limited visibility of low- and middle-income settings within this database warrants further investigation. Equity, implementation, and digital and resuscitative technologies are potential areas for further research; the pooled network analysis does not establish their temporal growth.

title: Outcomes after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Sex and age differences.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sex differences may affect outcomes after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), potentially mediated by estrogen, levels of which change with age. However, it remains unclear whether the impact of sex on outcomes varies across different age groups. This study aimed to examine sex- and age-related differences in neurological outcomes after ECPR for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA).
METHODS: This was a retrospective observational study using a nationwide, hospital-based, prospective registry of patients with OHCA in Japan. Adult patients with non-traumatic OHCA who received ECPR between 2014 and 2022 were included. Patients were divided into two age groups (<50 and ≥ 50 years) based on a cut-off used in a previous population-based study and the potential influence of age-related changes in estrogen exposure. The primary outcome was a 30-day favorable neurological outcome. Associations between sex and outcomes were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression with a sex-age group interaction term, adjusted for patient characteristics and prognostic clinical factors.
RESULTS: A total of 95,902 patients with OHCA were included in the registry, of whom 2844 (2310 men, 534 women) were adults, had experienced non-traumatic OHCA, and received ECPR. A total of 56 men and 16 women aged <50 years and 127 men and 29 women aged ≥50 years achieved a favorable neurological outcome. In the primary analysis, no significant differences were observed between men and women aged <50 years [adjusted OR 0.99 (0.52-1.79)] or aged ≥50 years [adjusted OR 1.21 (0.77-1.84)]. Furthermore, the interaction between sex and age group was not significant (p for interaction = 0.63).
CONCLUSIONS: No statistically significant differences in 30-day neurological outcomes between men and women were detected across age groups, and the sex-age group interaction was not statistically significant among patients who received ECPR after OHCA.

title: A national cross-sectional analysis of regional and rural-urban variation in emergency medical services naloxone administration for suspected opioid overdose.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Emergency medical services (EMS) naloxone administration is often used as a surveillance marker for overdose incidence, but whether administration during suspected opioid-overdose encounters varies geographically is less clear. This study examined regional and rural-urban variation in documented EMS naloxone administration.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis used the 2025 National Emergency Medical Services Information System public-release research dataset. The treatment-independent analytic cohort included adults aged 18-89 years with suspected opioid involvement, documented patient contact, and complete geographic exposure data. Multivariable logistic regression estimated associations of U.S. Census region and urbanicity with EMS-administered naloxone. Every model included naloxone before EMS arrival. The fully adjusted model included age, documented fentanyl and heroin involvement, race and ethnicity, naloxone before EMS arrival, cardiac arrest before arrival, and provider-assigned acuity. Sensitivity analyses addressed disposition, unit capability, an alternative ICD-based opioid-overdose definition, and naloxone administrations with documented improved response missed by the primary definition.
RESULTS: Among 110,261 activations, EMS administered naloxone in 37,412 (33.9%). In the clinically adjusted model, compared with the Northeast, adjusted odds of administration were higher in the South (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.10, 95% confidence interval [CI] [2.01, 2.18]), Midwest (aOR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.84, 2.01]), and West (aOR = 1.31, 95% CI [1.25, 1.37]). Corresponding adjusted probability differences were 15.2, 13.2, and 5.1 percentage points. The rural-versus-urban association attenuated to the null after clinical adjustment (aOR = 1.01, 95% CI [0.94, 1.09]). The regional pattern persisted across sensitivity analyses, although estimates attenuated in expanded cohorts.
CONCLUSIONS: Documented EMS naloxone administration during suspected opioid-overdose encounters varied substantially across U.S. Census regions, whereas rural-urban differences were smaller and less stable. The findings identify geographically patterned variation in documented treatment and support evaluation with agency-level data; they do not establish that every non-administration was clinically inappropriate.

title: Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Postarrest Cardiac Procedures for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Effective postarrest care facilitates optimal outcomes for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Relatively little research has evaluated whether there may be racial or ethnic disparities in the workup and management of the patient post arrest.
METHODS: We retrospectively studied out-of-hospital cardiac arrests using the TriNetX research database. We defined out-of-hospital cardiac arrest as any emergency department visit (2013-2024) with a diagnosis of cardiac arrest and included patients who survived to admission. Multivariate adjusted logistic regression was used to compare rates of the following cardiac interventions across race or ethnicity: (1) echocardiography; (2) left heart catheterization; (3) percutaneous coronary intervention; (4) ventricular assist device placement; and (5) automated implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement.
RESULTS: A total of 58 394 cases of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest met inclusion criteria. Compared with White patients (left heart catheterization: 13.9%, percutaneous coronary intervention: 7.1%, ventricular assist device: 3.0%, automated implantable cardioverter-defibrillator: 0.9%), Black patients had lower odds of receiving left heart catheterization (7.2%, adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.60 [95% CI, 0.55-0.64]), percutaneous coronary intervention (2.6%, aOR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.42-0.53]), ventricular assist device placement (1.6%, aOR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.60-0.80]), and automated implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement (0.4%, aOR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.41-0.70]). Hispanic/Latino patients were also less likely to receive left heart catheterization (8.9%, aOR, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.64-0.80]), percutaneous coronary intervention (3.7%, aOR, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.53-0.74]), and automated implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement (0.4%, aOR, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.33-0.81]).
CONCLUSIONS: Our large multicenter analysis identifies racial or ethnic disparities in postarrest cardiac workup and management. Further research is needed to identify potential causes for these disparities with the hope of developing strategies to address them.

title: Advanced Age in Acute Myocardial Infarction-Related Cardiogenic Shock by Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Status.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiogenic shock (CS) remains a leading cause of in-hospital mortality in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Although advanced age is associated with worse outcomes, associations across out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) strata remain incompletely characterized.
OBJECTIVES: The objective of the study was to evaluate the association between octogenarian status and in-hospital mortality in patients with AMI-related CS (AMI-CS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and to examine this association in analyses stratified by OHCA status.
METHODS: We analyzed patients with AMI-CS enrolled in the multicenter Kanagawa-ACuTe cardIoVascular rEgistry who underwent PCI. Octogenarian status (≥80 years) was the primary exposure. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate associations with in-hospital mortality, with additional analyses stratified by OHCA status.
RESULTS: Among 658 patients, 177 (26.9%) were octogenarians, and 279 (42.4%) died during hospitalization. Octogenarian status was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR: 2.14; 95% CI: 1.32-3.48; P = 0.002). In stratified analyses, octogenarian status was associated with higher mortality among patients without OHCA, whereas no statistically significant association was observed among those with OHCA. The interaction between octogenarian status and OHCA was not statistically significant (P for interaction = 0.422). Higher heart rate, unmeasurable heart rate, higher serum creatinine, and lower serum albumin were independently associated with mortality.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with AMI-CS undergoing PCI, octogenarian status was independently associated with in-hospital mortality. Although estimates differed numerically across OHCA strata, the interaction was not statistically significant, precluding a conclusion that the association differed according to OHCA status. These stratified findings should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Chronological age should be considered within a comprehensive clinical assessment rather than in isolation.

title: FAST Performance Changes After a Training Sequence Including Augmented Reality Guidance Among Paramedic Students.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Point-of-care ultrasound is an essential diagnostic tool in emergency medicine. Among its applications, Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) is a rapid imaging method used in initial trauma evaluation. Augmented reality (AR) may provide visual guidance during procedural learning. This study examined changes in FAST performance following a short-term training sequence that included AR-assisted guidance among paramedic students.
METHODS: An interventional study was conducted with 18 undergraduate paramedic students who participated in a two-hour program consisting of a 60-minute lecture and a 60-minute hands-on session. Each participant performed four FAST examinations: 2 conventional and 2 AR-assisted. The primary outcome was total FAST performance time; secondary outcomes were the time for each view and the Quality of Ultrasound Imaging and Competence score, including the Task-Specific Checklist and Global Rating Scale.
RESULTS: The median total FAST time was significantly reduced after the training sequence (difference: 263.5 s; 95% CI: 177-352.5; P<0.001). Significant time reductions were observed in the pericardial, Morison's pouch, and perisplenic views, but not in the Douglas pouch view. Both Task-Specific Checklist and Global Rating Scale scores improved significantly (both P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Improvements in procedural efficiency and technical performance were observed after a short training sequence that included AR-assisted guidance for FAST among paramedic students. Given the fixed examination sequence and absence of a parallel control group, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Rethinking Mild Therapeutic Hypothermia After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Dead End or Missed Opportunity? An Expert Viewpoint.
abstract: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains associated with high mortality and neurological disability. Mild therapeutic hypothermia has been questioned after large trials failed to demonstrate superiority over controlled normothermia with fever prevention. In this expert viewpoint, we argue that these neutral findings should not be interpreted as proof of biological futility in every patient and setting. The clinical effect of hypothermia may depend on patient phenotype, timing of initiation, cooling technique, temperature-control quality, and integration with contemporary post-resuscitation care. This may be particularly important in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention, in whom hypothermia can impair the pharmacokinetics and antiplatelet effects of oral P2Y12 inhibitors. Current evidence does not support routine hypothermia in all comatose survivors. However, uncertainty remains regarding its value in selected patients. Patients with an intermediate degree of ischemic brain injury may represent a plausible target for neuroprotection, but this remains an unproven hypothesis. Future trials should investigate whether injury severity modifies the effects of early, precisely delivered hypothermia, using standardized protocols, active normothermia as the comparator, and prespecified antithrombotic and post-resuscitation strategies.

title: Prehospital Cold-Water Immersion for Undifferentiated Heat Stroke: A Case Series.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Heat stroke is a time-sensitive condition that requires early intervention to prevent morbidity and mortality. Heat-related deaths are also increasing. Multiple studies have evaluated various cooling methods and assessed their effectiveness, safety, and practicality across diverse settings and populations. Earlier and faster cooling leads to improved patient outcomes. The National Association of Emergency Medical Services Physicians recommends initiating prehospital cold-water immersion before emergency medical services (EMS) transport.
CASE SERIES: This case series evaluated the feasibility and effectiveness of prehospital cold-water immersion initiated before and continued during EMS transportation from the scene to emergency department arrival in this critically ill patient population.
CONCLUSION: Rapid initiation and maintenance of prehospital cold-water immersion in undifferentiated heat stroke was both feasible and effective. Over the course of the case series, no deaths were reported, and all patients were eventually discharged home.

title: On-Scene Time-Dependent Probabilities of Return of Spontaneous Circulation and Favorable Neurological Outcome in Cases of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with an Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Retrospective Study Using the National Utstein Data in Japan.
abstract: Background/Objectives: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with an initial shockable rhythm, the likelihood of achieving on-scene return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and favorable neurological outcomes changes with elapsed resuscitation time. We aimed to describe these time-dependent patterns under existing Japanese emergency medical services (EMS) practice. Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective descriptive cohort study using linked Japanese Utstein and emergency transport data from 2017-2022. Adults with cardiogenic OHCA and an initial shockable rhythm were included. For each time point after EMS contact, we calculated the observed probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC and, among patients achieving on-scene ROSC, the probability of a favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2 at 1 month) according to ROSC timing. Results: Among 22,383 eligible patients, 5095 achieved on-scene ROSC and 3182 had favorable neurological outcomes. The probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC was 6.97% (1295/18,583; 95% CI, 6.61-7.34%) at 10 min and 0.50% (87/17,375; 95% CI, 0.41-0.62%) at 20 min. At 10 min, favorable neurological outcomes occurred in 50.0% of patients aged <75 years and 20.5% of those aged ≥75 years who achieved on-scene ROSC at or after that time point. A sensitivity analysis restricted to 3128 patients receiving first EMS defibrillation within 1 min showed broadly similar temporal patterns. Conclusions: Under existing Japanese EMS practice, subsequent on-scene ROSC and favorable neurological outcomes became less frequent with later ROSC timing. Younger patients showed more favorable neurological outcomes at later ROSC times, but these findings do not establish age-based criteria for prolonged resuscitation or transport decisions.

title: Predicting survival in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Development and internal validation of risk scores.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the pediatric population is associated with poor survival and neurological outcomes. We aimed to develop and internally validate risk scores to predict survival to discharge in pediatric OHCA patients.
METHODS: We included pediatric OHCA patients in the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival from 2013 to 2023. We used logistic regression (LR) and classification and regression trees (CART) to develop risk scores using 70% of the data and validated them using the remaining 30% of the data. We used discrimination and predictive accuracy to evaluate model performance.
RESULTS: We included 26,895 pediatric patients, of whom 27.8% survived to hospital admission and 11.9% survived to hospital discharge. We developed three separate risk scores for i) infants ii) preschool and school-age children, and iii) adolescents. The most important predictor variables were gender, arrest location, witness status, etiology of arrest, bystander CPR, use of prehospital AED, and first rhythm. Models developed using both LR and CART approaches had good classification accuracy (AUROCC for LR: 0.81, 0.77 and 0.82, AUROCC for CART: 0.78, 0.76, 0.82 for the three age groups) However, we found CART models to be the most useful because they are simpler to follow, classified more patients in low and high survival categories using a smaller number of predictors. The average survival probability in infants for each risk group was 3%, 13%, and 33%, for preschool and school-age children it was 4%, 11%, and 29%, whereas for adolescents it was 4%, 13%, and 48% for the low, moderate, and high survival categories.
CONCLUSION: Pediatric patients experiencing OHCA can be classified into low, moderate, and high survival categories using a simple risk score and easily identified prehospital variables. These risk scores can facilitate research, monitor the quality of medical services and can potentially support clinical decision-making.
