title: Heat stroke-induced liver injury: mechanistic insights, immune dynamics, and emerging therapeutic targets.
abstract: Heat stroke is a life-threatening heat-related emergency that often leads to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), with liver injury among its most prominent manifestations. HS-associated acute liver injury (HS-ALI) is a major determinant of prognosis, yet its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests that HS-ALI results from the interplay of direct thermal stress, systemic inflammation, oxidative imbalance, coagulation dysfunction, and regulated cell death. Emerging experimental studies have implicated pyroptosis, ferroptosis, necroptosis, and gut-liver immune crosstalk in HS-associated tissue injury; however, the strength of evidence varies considerably among these mechanisms, and direct validation in human HS-ALI remains limited. Accordingly, these pathways should be considered potential contributors to disease progression rather than uniformly established mechanisms.

title: Built environment and emergency medical services response time in a high-density megacity: multilevel evidence from urban-suburban.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Emergency medical services (EMS) response time is a key indicator for evaluating the performance of public health system and is closely associated with patient survival rates. However, empirical evidence on the potential relationship between the built environment and EMS response time remains limited, restricting the development of spatially informed strategies for improving EMS system operations.
METHODS: This study employed 2024 ambulance dispatch data from the Beijing Emergency Center Office Management System, combined with multi-source data on the built environment, to construct a multilevel regression model examining the influence of subdistrict (township)-level built environment factors on EMS response time and investigating the heterogeneity between urban areas and suburbs.
RESULTS: The results indicate that, at the citywide level, lower residential facility density and denser arterial and local road networks significantly reduced EMS response time. Specifically, while in central urban areas, high densities of residential facilities were associated with longer response time, in suburban areas, higher densities of local roads enhanced EMS efficiency.
DISCUSSION: These findings provide valuable evidence to guide built environment interventions aimed at shortening EMS response time and improving service efficiency across different areas.

title: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest as the First Manifestation of ALCAPA in a 9-Week-Old Infant: Survival to Discharge After Emergency Repair and VA-ECMO.
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) usually presents with heart failure at 2-3 months of age; cardiac arrest as the first manifestation is rare and often recognized only at autopsy. Case Presentation: A previously healthy girl collapsed at home at 65 days of age. After dispatcher-assisted parental resuscitation, the emergency team found asystole and achieved return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 4 min of professional resuscitation; the total low-flow time was not recorded. She was in cardiogenic shock (left ventricular ejection fraction 19.8%, high-sensitivity troponin T 2620 ng/L) with acute kidney injury and coagulopathy consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Echocardiography showed a dilated right coronary artery and no flow from the aorta into the left coronary artery. Emergency repair on day 1 was followed by venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for 4 days and continuous renal replacement therapy. The Simpson ejection fraction reached about 50% by day 9, fell to 37-40% during respiratory deterioration and was 45-50% on day 27; mitral regurgitation, graded as massive during VA-ECMO, regressed to trace without valve surgery. She was discharged on day 42 with impaired diastolic indices; no formal neurological assessment was documented. Conclusions: ALCAPA should be considered in every infant with unexplained cardiac arrest, and post-resuscitation echocardiography should assess the coronary origins. Emergency repair with VA-ECMO can achieve survival to discharge despite multiorgan failure, but long-term cardiac and neurodevelopmental follow-up is required.

title: Effect modification by arterial pH on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with shockable rhythm: A multicenter registry study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Arterial pH on emergency department (ED) arrival predicts outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its effect on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and neurological outcomes is unclear. We evaluated this association in patients with an initial shockable rhythm and assessed whether pH modified it.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed the Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium registry. Adults with presumed cardiac-origin OHCA, an initial shockable rhythm, ED cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and arterial blood gas data measured after ED arrival were included. Exposure was ECPR initiated in the ED; the primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome at discharge (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2). Arterial pH was categorized as low (≤6.85), medium (>6.85 and <7.05), or high (≥7.05). Multivariable logistic regression assessed ECPR-by-pH interaction, with optimal 1:2 propensity score matching as a sensitivity analysis.
RESULTS: Of 2183 patients, 213 (9.8%) received ECPR and 154 (7.1%) had a favorable neurological outcome. The association between ECPR and favorable outcome differed across pH categories (p for interaction = 0.004): adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 7.34 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.84-18.98) in the low-pH group, 2.07 (95% CI, 1.06-4.03) in the medium-pH group, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.37-1.94) in the high-pH group. The propensity score-matched analysis showed a similar pattern (p for interaction = 0.036).
CONCLUSIONS: Initial arterial pH modified the association between ECPR and neurological outcome after OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm. The association was strongest at low pH and not observed at high pH. Arterial pH may inform ECPR evaluation but should not determine treatment thresholds.

title: Admission arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a single-centre retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Admission arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) is readily available after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its independent prognostic value is uncertain and prior evidence is conflicting. We evaluated the association of admission PaCO2 with one-month mortality and neurological outcome, and quantified its incremental prognostic value.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: In a single-center retrospective cohort of 617 adults resuscitated from OHCA (2014-2023), patients were stratified by admission PaCO2 (≤50, >50-70 and >70 mmHg). The primary outcome was one-month all-cause mortality; the secondary outcome was neurological status at one month by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC), analyzed as a dichotomous, ordinal and survivor-restricted endpoint. Associations were estimated with multivariable logistic and ordinal regression adjusted for age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), call-to-arrival time, initial shockable rhythm, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and arrest etiology. PaCO2 was modelled continuously (per 10 mmHg) and categorically; sensitivity analyses used alternative cut-points, and discrimination was quantified by the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC). A simplified Directed Acyclic Graph was used heuristically for variable selection; however, we explicitly acknowledge that post-resuscitation physiology represents a complex feedback system. Therefore, formal causal effect estimation was not attempted, and all analyses are strictly associational and prognostic.
RESULTS: One-month mortality was 73.6% (454/617) and rose across PaCO2 groups (49.7%, 81.1%, and 90.7%; p < 0.001). Each 10-mmHg increase in PaCO2 was associated with higher mortality after adjustment for measured confounders (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.45, 95% CI 1.24-1.70; p < 0.001), with a concordant gradient for the ordinal CPC outcome (common aOR 1.53, 95% CI 1.31-1.79) and among survivors (aOR 1.91, 95% CI 1.25-2.91). The graded association was robust across categorization schemes but was attenuated after additional adjustment for concurrent acid-base and gas-exchange markers (lactate, base excess, PaO2; aOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.64-1.01; p = 0.063), consistent with strong collinearity between PaCO2 and acid-base status. Adding PaCO2 to a clinical model produced a minimal incremental improvement in discrimination of uncertain clinical utility (AUC 0.794 to 0.816; ΔAUC 0.022, 95% CI 0.002-0.043; optimism-corrected AUC 0.802). Calibration was assessed via bootstrap validation (calibration slope: 0.98, 95% CI 0.89-1.07; calibration-in-the-large: -0.04, 95% CI -0.21 to 0.13), indicating adequate agreement between predicted and observed risks.
CONCLUSIONS: In this decade-long cohort, higher admission PaCO2 was associated with increased one-month mortality and worse neurological outcome after OHCA, but added minimal discrimination beyond established clinical factors. Because admission PaCO2 is a treatment-dependent exposure - determined by CPR duration and quality, airway and ventilation management, ventilator settings and the ROSC-to-sampling interval, none of which were available - independent prognostic value cannot be established from these data, and the association is most plausibly a signal of arrest severity and of the resuscitation delivered. Attenuation after adjustment for metabolic acidosis is consistent with shared pathophysiology, although mediator overadjustment cannot be excluded. Admission PaCO2 is immediate, inexpensive and universally available, but prospective studies capturing resuscitation timings, CPR quality and standardized ventilation are required before any prognostic role can be claimed.

title: Circadian rhythmicity in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: a scoping review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) are time-critical events that exhibit circadian patterns, which influence their incidence and clinical outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether circadian rhythmicity influences the time of onset of OHCA and STEMI, as well as related clinical outcomes, in patients requiring prehospital emergency care and subsequent hospitalization.
DESIGN: A scoping review.
METHODS: The search process included four online databases: MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL Plus with Full Text, ScienceDirect, and ProQuest. The review included original articles published between January 2010 and December 2024.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies met the inclusion criteria. These revealed that the incidence of OHCA and STEMI exhibits significant circadian variability, with the highest incidence in the morning. OHCA often has a secondary afternoon/evening peak. The nighttime hours are associated with the lowest incidence. Patients with nighttime OHCA or STEMI have a lower probability of return of spontaneous circulation and worse one-month and one-year survival and neurological outcomes. This less favorable prognosis is not due to the time of day when the event occurs but rather due to limited bystander availability, lower rates of bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation, and longer times to hospital intervention. Additionally, these events were more frequently recorded in winter, while weekly variations were insignificant.
CONCLUSION: Circadian and seasonal factors influence the occurrence and clinical course of OHCA and STEMI, with worse outcomes for nighttime cases being more a consequence of limited availability than the time of the event itself.

title: Longer collapse-to-first-medical-contact interval is independently associated with ROSC in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a paradoxical finding that may reflect case-mix differences.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shortening prehospital time intervals is a cornerstone of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) management, with earlier medical contact generally assumed to improve survival. However, this assumption has rarely been scrutinized at the level of individual time metrics, particularly the interval from witnessed collapse to first medical contact (collapse-to-FMC), whose relationship with resuscitation outcomes independent of case-mix remains unclear. This study aimed to examine the association between core prehospital time intervals and the achievement of prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 152 consecutive OHCA patients managed by the Cixi Emergency Center between April 2023 and March 2026. Time intervals were derived from synchronized dispatch center logs and onboard system timestamps, including dispatch-to-scene arrival, collapse-to-first medical contact, and collapse-to-CPR initiation intervals. Candidate variables for multivariable modeling were selected based on a prespecified causal rationale and clinical relevance, rather than solely on univariate statistical significance. Univariate logistic regression was performed for descriptive purposes to examine crude associations with prehospital ROSC. The main model included the two core time intervals (collapse-to-FMC and collapse-to-CPR initiation). Model 1 further adjusted for age, a clinically important confounder that did not reach statistical significance in univariate analysis. Model 2 additionally adjusted for etiology of arrest and presence of a shockable rhythm, which were selected a priori as pre-exposure confounders based on established prognostic importance in OHCA research. This approach ensured that clinically important confounders were retained regardless of their univariate P values. A main model included only time variables, and an adjusted model further incorporated clinical covariates. Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors, and model calibration was evaluated with the Hosmer-Lemeshow test. Discriminative ability was assessed by receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed by age (<65 vs. ≥65 years) and etiology (cardiac vs. non-cardiac).
RESULTS: Among 152 patients, 52 (34.2%) achieved prehospital ROSC. Conventional dispatch-related intervals did not differ between groups. The collapse-to-first medical contact interval was significantly longer in the ROSC group (20.0 vs. 13.1 min, P < 0.001) and remained independently associated with ROSC after adjustment for prespecified pre-exposure confounders, including age, etiology of arrest, and presence of a shockable rhythm (OR 1.188, 95% CI: 1.079-1.307, P < 0.001). Bootstrap internal validation yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.882 (95% CI: 0.827-0.936), with a calibration intercept of -0.063, a calibration slope of 0.972, and a Brier score of 0.132, indicating adequate calibration. In subgroup analyses, this association was predominantly observed in patients younger than 65 years (adjusted P = 0.037), and the interval from collapse to CPR initiation became significant in the cardiac etiology subgroup after adjustment (OR 1.567, 95% CI: 1.054-2.329, P = 0.026).
CONCLUSION: In this cohort of OHCA patients, a longer collapse-to-first medical contact interval was paradoxically associated with increased odds of prehospital ROSC, independent of prespecified pre-exposure confounders. This counterintuitive finding suggests that the interval may reflect patient salvageability and unmeasured case-mix characteristics rather than treatment delay alone. These results challenge the conventional premise that shorter time to medical contact uniformly translates to better outcomes, and underscore the need for a more nuanced understanding of how patient characteristics shape the relationship between prehospital timing and resuscitation success.

title: Emergency medical services personnel's work capability sets: associations with job demands, job resources, and flourishing at work.
abstract: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel perform complex and demanding work under challenging conditions while providing essential healthcare services. Understanding the factors that support their flourishing at work is important for their sustainable employability and the functioning of healthcare systems. This study investigated EMS personnel's work capability sets (enabled and achieved valued work outcomes) and their associations with job demands (emotional demands and work pressure), job resources (autonomy at work and co-worker support), flourishing at work (emotional, psychological, and social well-being), and negative affect. A cross-sectional survey design was used with 197 EMS personnel in South Africa. Participants completed the Job Demands-Resources Questionnaire, the Capability Set for Work Questionnaire, and the Flourishing at Work-Short Form. Correlation analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, latent class analysis, and Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars analyses were conducted. Using knowledge and skills, developing knowledge and skills, and building and maintaining meaningful relationships at work emerged as the strongest work capabilities, whereas earning a good income, involvement in important decisions, and contributing to something valuable were the weakest. Latent class analysis identified three distinct capability sets: a weak capability set (48%), a constrained capability set (30%), and a robust capability set (22%). Emotional demands were negatively associated with work capabilities and flourishing and positively associated with negative affect, whereas work pressure was positively associated with negative affect but not significantly associated with overall work capabilities or flourishing. Job demands did not significantly differentiate the capability sets, whereas autonomy and co-worker support did. EMS personnel in the robust capability set reported greater flourishing and lower negative affect than those in the weak capability set. The findings are consistent with the Sustainable Employability model grounded in the Capability Approach showing that broader capability sets are associated with greater flourishing at work. Strengthening enabling work conditions, particularly autonomy and co-worker support, while attending to demands that may constrain work capabilities, may help create conditions conducive to the realization of valued work outcomes, flourishing, and sustainable employability among EMS personnel.

title: Modelled Response Times for Police and Fire Brigade Co-Dispatch to Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Geospatial Simulation Study in Vorarlberg, Austria.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) depends on the interval between collapse and the start of chest compressions. We estimated how co-dispatching police and volunteer fire brigades alongside emergency medical services (EMS) would change the modelled time from dispatch to arrival of the first unit in Vorarlberg, Austria. Methods: In a geospatial simulation, 500 OHCA locations were drawn from a 100 m population raster, weighted by residential population. Driving times from all 18 EMS, 28 police and 121 volunteer fire stations were routed on the road network, and turnout times of 2 min (EMS), 0 min (police) and 5 min (fire brigade) were added; all units were modelled as continuously available at fixed stations. Four configurations (EMS alone, EMS plus police, EMS plus fire brigade, triple dispatch) were compared by paired time gains and 10 min coverage with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs); uncertainty from sampling, turnout times, unit availability and routing was assessed separately. Results: Of 500 missions, 499 were analysable. Median response time was 9.81 min with EMS alone, 5.45 min with EMS plus police, 7.36 min with EMS plus fire brigade and 5.41 min with triple dispatch; the paired median time gain of triple dispatch over EMS alone was 4.34 min (95% CI 3.80-4.67). Locations reached within 10 min rose from 51.1% to 87.4%, 87.0% and 94.6%, and the resident population inside the 10 min isochrones rose from 55.6% to 90.9%, 91.9% and 95.5%. Conclusions: Under fixed station locations, continuous unit availability and assumed agency-specific turnout times, police and fire brigade co-dispatch increased modelled ten-minute coverage compared with EMS alone. Police arrived earlier at most locations, whereas the denser fire station network contributed most in rural areas; their combination reached the most locations. Operational validation is required before these estimates can inform regional implementation.

title: Frequent Callers to Emergency Medical Services: an observational cohort study from Region Zealand, Denmark (2018-2025).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Frequent callers to Emergency Medical Services represent a small group of citizens who account for a substantial number of calls. Despite their impact, little is known about their characteristics and patterns of EMS use. This study aimed to examine frequency, dispatch outcomes, and characteristics of frequent callers in a prehospital setting.
METHODS: We conducted an observational cohort study of calls to the Emergency Medical Dispatch Center in Region Zealand, Denmark, between 2018 and 2025. Calls without a civil register number and individuals younger than 18 years were excluded. Frequent callers were defined as individuals contacting 1-1-2 five or more times within 12 consecutive months. Calls from frequent callers were categorized as pre-frequent calls (before reaching the threshold) and post-threshold calls (from the fifth call onward). Descriptive statistics were used to compare frequent callers with non-frequent callers, as well as subgroups of frequent callers based on call frequency.
RESULTS: Overall, 214 091 individuals made 443 977 calls. Of these, 3.0% (n = 6 415) were frequent callers, accounting for 19.9% (n = 88 260) of all calls. "Unclear problem" was the most common contact cause across all groups, whereas "Alcohol/intoxication/overdose" and "Psychiatry - Suicidal" were only among the five most common contact causes in the post-threshold groups with the highest call volumes. High-priority dispatch was assigned to 89.6% of non-frequent calls, 84.3% of pre-frequent calls, and 73.1% of post-threshold calls. Telephone resolution without ambulance dispatch increased across groups (7.3%, 12.5%, and 23.8%, respectively), as did non-conveyance after dispatch (19.2%, 20.8%, and 27.4%). Differences became more pronounced with increasing post-threshold call volume.
CONCLUSIONS: Frequent callers accounted for a substantial proportion of contacts to the Emergency Medical Dispatch Center. While pre-frequent calls resembled calls from non-frequent callers, post-threshold calls were more often resolved over the phone and less often resulted in hospital transport.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Approval for performance of the study was given by the Emergency Medical Services in Region Zealand (p202519525).

title: An ecological time-series study of heat-related illness in Honolulu County, Hawai'i: implications for heat preparedness and public health response.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heat-related illness (HRI) is a growing public health concern. HRI risk in Hawai'i has not previously been reviewed to determine the risks of heat on public health and well-being. This study summarizes HRI in Honolulu County and evaluates the relationship between local daily heat metrics and HRI by residency status.
METHODS: Syndromic surveillance was used to collect clinical visits to hospital emergency departments, urgent care centers, and outpatient clinics for HRI in Honolulu County from January 2022 to December 2024. Associations between daily maximum heat metrics (dry bulb, wet bulb, and heat index) and HRI were estimated using Poisson regression with distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs). Models incorporated a 3-day cumulative lag and were adjusted for temporal trends and day of the week, with relative risks estimated by comparing the 75th to the 25th percentile of each heat metric.
RESULTS: During the study period, the syndromic surveillance system captured 969 HRI cases in Honolulu County; 698 (72.0%) occurred in residents and 271 (28.0%) in visitors. Daily maximum dry bulb, wet bulb, and heat index temperatures showed seasonal variation. In DLNMs, dry bulb temperature was not significantly associated with HRI. In contrast, higher wet bulb temperature was associated with increased HRI risk for both residents (RR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.21-2.12) and visitors (RR = 2.54, 95% CI: 1.66-3.90), and higher heat index was also associated with increased risk for residents (RR = 2.13, 95% CI: 1.36-3.34) and visitors (RR = 2.68, 95% CI: 1.33-5.41).
CONCLUSIONS: HRIs in Honolulu County were strongly associated with heat metrics that incorporate humidity. Consistent with previous studies, these results highlight the importance of accounting for both temperature and humidity when assessing the risk of heat stress, as humidity-inclusive metrics may better guide heat-related public health prevention and preparedness efforts in humid climates such as Hawai'i. Because meteorological exposures were derived from a single monitoring station representing county level conditions, these findings should be interpreted at the county level and may not fully capture localized microclimatic variability across O'ahu.

title: Prehospital endotracheal intubation and return of spontaneous circulation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients: a retrospective cohort study based on prehospital emergency registry data.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The optimal airway strategy during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain. This study investigated the association between prehospital endotracheal intubation (ETI) and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) using a regional emergency medical services registry.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study analyzed 6,162 adult non-traumatic OHCA patients treated by emergency medical services between October 2023 and November 2024. Patients were categorized into an ETI group (n = 1,448) and a basic airway (BA) group (n = 4,714). The primary outcome was prehospital ROSC. Long-term survival and neurological outcomes were not available in the registry. Multivariable logistic regression and propensity score-matched sensitivity analysis were used to evaluate the association between ETI and ROSC while accounting for measured confounders. Airway strategy was selected by on-scene physicians during routine EMS care, and rhythm-stratified unadjusted analyses were performed to describe whether the ETI-ROSC association differed by initial rhythm category.
RESULTS: ROSC occurred more frequently in the ETI group than in the BA group (21.1% vs. 3.8%, P < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, ETI was strongly associated with ROSC (OR = 7.61, 95% CI: 6.07-9.53, P < 0.001). Shockable initial rhythm (OR = 5.42, 95% CI: 3.80-7.74, P < 0.001) and defibrillation (OR = 1.82, 95% CI: 1.37-2.42, P < 0.001) were also positively associated with ROSC, whereas longer response time and epinephrine administration were negatively associated with ROSC. In 1:1 propensity score-matched analysis, the association between ETI and ROSC remained significant (OR = 6.33, 95% CI: 4.72-8.47, P < 0.001). Rhythm-stratified analyses showed that the unadjusted association was strongest in non-shockable and other/unknown rhythm strata and was not statistically significant in the shockable rhythm stratum.
CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective prehospital registry cohort, ETI during OHCA resuscitation was strongly associated with higher ROSC rates. Because airway timing relative to collapse and ROSC, survival to discharge, and neurological outcomes were not captured, these findings should be interpreted as an association with immediate resuscitation success rather than evidence of a causal survival benefit. The observed association may also reflect physician selection of airway strategy and other unmeasured resuscitation factors, and should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating.
